overview.title: Bidirectional RNNs: order dependence and the reversed-sequence experiment
overview.main_topic: Introduction of bidirectional RNNs; RNNs' order dependence; the experiment of feeding reversed (antichronological) sequences to the LSTM, which underperforms the commonsense baseline on weather data; why reversed order works as well as forward order on text; why different-yet-useful representations are worth exploiting
overview.central_idea: RNNs are order-sensitive, so running one forward and one backward over the same sequence yields two different representations. On weather forecasting, the reversed direction is much worse because the recent past is most predictive and the LSTM remembers recent inputs best. On text, either order works, so the two directions give different but equally useful views, which is what a bidirectional RNN exploits.
overview.importance: It explains when bidirectional RNNs help (text, where which order you use is not crucial) and when they don't (the Jena task, as Listing 13.24 on p.402 confirms). It also introduces a general machine learning principle (diverse but useful representations improve performance) that leads to ensembling (chapter 18).
learning_objectives: Define a bidirectional RNN: two regular RNNs over the same sequence in chronological and antichronological order, with merged representations.
Explain what 'RNNs are order dependent' means and why it makes them good for timeseries.
Describe the reversed-sequence experiment and its outcome on the Jena task.
Explain why the reversed LSTM underperforms on weather data (recency of useful information plus the LSTM's bias toward recent inputs).
Explain why reversed processing works about as well as forward on text.
State the principle that different yet useful representations are worth exploiting.
prerequisites: How an RNN processes a sequence step by step with a state (p.389-391)
The first LSTM model and the commonsense baseline (p.384, p.388)

summary:
**13.3.6 Using bidirectional RNNs.** The last technique of the section. A **bidirectional RNN** is a common RNN variant that can outperform a regular RNN on certain tasks; it is frequently used in natural language processing, 'the Swiss Army knife of deep learning for natural language processing'.

**Order dependence.** RNNs process timesteps in order, so shuffling or reversing them can completely change the representations extracted. That is why RNNs do well where order matters, as in temperature forecasting. A bidirectional RNN *exploits* this order sensitivity: it uses two regular RNNs (e.g. `GRU` or `LSTM`), one processing the sequence chronologically and the other antichronologically, and merges their representations, so it can catch patterns a unidirectional RNN may overlook.

**Was chronological order arbitrary?** So far all RNNs here processed sequences oldest-first, a decision 'we made no attempt to question'. To test it, reverse the input sequences along the time axis (`samples[:, ::-1, :]`). Training the same LSTM model as in the first experiment on reversed data, you would find it **strongly underperforms even the commonsense baseline**. So chronological processing matters here, and it makes sense: an LSTM is typically better at remembering the recent past than the distant past, and recent weather data is more predictive than older data (which is also why the commonsense baseline is fairly strong). Reading in reverse puts the most useful data furthest from the output.

**Text is different.** For many other problems, including natural language, a word's importance does not depend strongly on its position in the sentence. On text, reversed processing works just as well as chronological: 'you can read text backwards just fine'. Word order matters, but *which order* you use is not crucial.

**Different but useful.** An RNN trained on reversed sequences learns different representations, as you would have different mental models if time ran backward and you were born on your last day. In machine learning, representations that are *different* yet *useful* are always worth exploiting, and the more they differ, the better (continued on p.402, which links this to ensembling).

paragraphs.excerpt: The last technique introduced in this section is called bidirectional RNNs. A bidirectional
paragraphs.what_it_says: Bidirectional RNNs are the last technique of the section: a common RNN variant that can outperform a regular RNN on certain tasks, frequently used in natural language processing, 'the Swiss Army knife of deep learning for natural language processing'.
paragraphs.what_it_means: 'On certain tasks' is an important qualifier: as the page goes on to show, the weather task is not one of them. NLP is where bidirectionality shines, because the meaning of a word depends on both its left and right context.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It completes the list announced on p.396 and sets expectations: this technique is mainly about text.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: before Transformers, bidirectional LSTMs were the standard encoder for tagging, classification and translation models; ELMo (2018) used bidirectional LSTM language models to produce contextual embeddings.

terminology.meaning: Two RNNs reading the same sequence in opposite directions, with their outputs merged.

connections: p.396: the roadmap listing bidirectional recurrent layers as the third technique.
p.402: Figure 13.13 and the Keras Bidirectional layer.

paragraphs.excerpt: RNNs are notably order dependent: they process the timesteps of their input sequences
paragraphs.what_it_says: RNNs are order dependent: they process timesteps in order, and shuffling or reversing them can completely change the extracted representations. That is why they work well where order matters, such as temperature forecasting. A bidirectional RNN exploits this: two regular RNNs (GRU or LSTM), one chronological, one antichronological, whose representations are merged, catching patterns a unidirectional RNN may miss.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Order dependence is a double-edged property. It is what lets an RNN model causality and recency (unlike the flattened Dense model or the pooled ConvNet of section 13.2). But it also means a single RNN gives one particular view of the sequence. Running a second RNN backward gives another view, and because the two are different, combining them can add information.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This is the core definition of a bidirectional RNN and the reason it can help: diversity of representations.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: with return_sequences=True, the forward RNN's output at step t summarizes x_1..x_t and the backward RNN's output at step t summarizes x_t..x_T, so their concatenation at t has context from the whole sequence. This is why bidirectional RNNs suit tagging tasks where each position needs both left and right context.

terminology.meaning: Oldest timestep first / newest timestep first.
An ordinary RNN reading in one direction only.

connections: p.388: why the Dense and Conv1D approaches failed: they destroyed order information.
p.628: RNNs suit sequences where patterns aren't invariant by temporal translation.

paragraphs.excerpt: Remarkably, the fact that the RNN layers in this section have processed sequences
paragraphs.what_it_says: Processing sequences in chronological order (oldest first) may have been an arbitrary decision, one the authors never questioned. Could the RNNs perform well on antichronological (newest-first) sequences? To test it, write a variant of the data pipeline that reverses the input sequences along the time dimension (the text says: replace the last line of the data generator with yield samples[:, ::-1, :], targets).
paragraphs.what_it_means: samples has shape (batch, timesteps, features); ::-1 on axis 1 reverses time while leaving the batch and feature axes untouched. The target is unchanged: still the temperature 24 hours after the end of the original sequence. Only the reading order changes. (In this edition the datasets come from timeseries_dataset_from_array, so the practical way is to map the dataset; there is no generator to edit.)
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It is a simple, informative ablation: questioning an implicit assumption with an experiment.

terminology.meaning: Changing one aspect of a setup (here, the input order) to measure its effect.

p.388: the LSTM model used in the first experiment.

paragraphs.excerpt: When training the same LSTM-based model that you used in the first experiment
paragraphs.what_it_says: Training the first-experiment LSTM on reversed sequences, you would find it strongly underperforms even the commonsense baseline, so chronological processing is important here. This makes sense: the LSTM typically remembers the recent past better than the distant past, and recent weather data is more predictive than older data (which is what makes the commonsense baseline fairly strong). So the chronological version is bound to outperform the reversed one.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Two facts combine. (1) The task: the best single predictor is the most recent temperature (the baseline uses only that). (2) The model: an LSTM's final output is dominated by inputs near the end of what it has read; information from early steps fades. Read chronologically, the most predictive data is the last thing seen. Read in reverse, it is the first thing seen, 120 steps before the output, and has largely faded. The reversed LSTM therefore cannot even match a predictor that just copies the latest temperature.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It predicts the result of Listing 13.24 on p.402: a bidirectional LSTM doesn't beat a plain LSTM on this task because its backward half is weak and it doubles capacity, causing earlier overfitting.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: 'better at remembering the recent past' is a soft bias, not a hard limit; the carry can preserve information over long ranges, but the gradients and the final state are still dominated by recent steps in practice.

terminology.meaning: The tendency of an RNN's output to depend most on the most recent inputs.

connections: p.383-384: the commonsense baseline: the temperature 24 hours later equals the current temperature.
p.402: the bidirectional LSTM underperforms the plain LSTM for this reason.

paragraphs.excerpt: However, this isn’t true for many other problems, including natural language: intuitively,
paragraphs.what_it_says: For many other problems, including natural language, a word's importance in understanding a sentence doesn't depend strongly on its position. On text, reversed-order processing works just as well as chronological; you can read text backwards just fine. Word order matters for language, but which order you use isn't crucial.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The distinction is between 'order matters' (permuting words changes meaning) and 'direction matters' (reading left-to-right is privileged). Weather forecasting has both: the target is in the future, at the end. Text classification has the first but not the second: the relevant cues can be anywhere, so neither direction is privileged.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This is the condition under which a bidirectional RNN is worthwhile: data where order matters but which order you use does not (p.402).

terminology.meaning: A task's indifference to whether a sequence is read forward or backward, while still caring about relative order.

connections: p.402: bidirectional RNNs are a great fit for text data.

paragraphs.excerpt: Importantly, an RNN trained on reversed sequences will learn different representations than one
paragraphs.what_it_says: An RNN trained on reversed sequences learns different representations from one trained on the original sequences, much as you would have different mental models if time flowed backward, living a life where you died on your first day and were born on your last. Representations that are different yet useful are always worth exploiting, and the more they differ (sentence continues on p.402: the better).
paragraphs.what_it_means: Even when both directions perform equally well (text), they do not learn the same features. Combining two good but different views gives a richer representation than either alone, because their errors are not identical.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This is the general principle behind bidirectional RNNs and, as p.402 says, behind ensembling (chapter 18).
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: in ensemble terms, averaging predictors whose errors are partly uncorrelated reduces variance; the reduction grows as their correlation decreases, which is the precise sense of 'the more they differ, the better' (as long as each stays useful).

terminology.meaning: Combining several models' predictions to improve on each individual model (chapter 18).

connections: p.402: the sentence concludes: the more they differ, the better; the intuition behind ensembling.

concepts.name: Bidirectional RNN
concepts.definition: Two regular RNNs (e.g. GRU or LSTM) processing the same input sequence chronologically and antichronologically, with their representations merged.
concepts.intuition: Reading a sentence once left-to-right and once right-to-left, then pooling what you learned.
concepts.technical: In Keras, layers.Bidirectional(layer) creates a second, separate instance of the given recurrent layer for the reversed direction (p.402).
concepts.significance: The 'Swiss Army knife' of deep learning for NLP; not helpful for the Jena task.
concepts.misconception: That bidirectional is always better than unidirectional; on the weather task the backward half is weak and the extra capacity causes earlier overfitting (p.402).

concepts.name: Order dependence of RNNs
concepts.definition: RNNs process timesteps in order, so shuffling or reversing them can completely change the representations extracted.
concepts.intuition: A story told out of order is a different story.
concepts.technical: The state at step t is a function of x_1..x_t in that order; permuting inputs changes every intermediate state.
concepts.significance: Why RNNs fit ordered problems like forecasting, and why two directions give two different views.
concepts.example: The reversed-order LSTM strongly underperforms the baseline on Jena.
concepts.misconception: That 'order matters' implies 'only one direction works'; for text, both directions work.

concepts.name: Commonsense baseline
concepts.definition: Predicting the temperature 24 hours from now as equal to the current temperature.
concepts.technical: Its strength shows that the most recent data is the most predictive, which is why the reversed LSTM fails.
concepts.significance: The reversed LSTM 'strongly underperforms even' this.
concepts.misconception: That a trivial baseline is easy to beat; on this task it took an LSTM to beat it.

concepts.name: Ensembling (preview)
concepts.definition: Combining different models or representations to boost performance.
concepts.intuition: Several witnesses with different viewpoints give a more reliable account than one.
concepts.technical: Works best when components are individually useful and as different as possible; covered in chapter 18.
concepts.significance: The principle behind why bidirectional RNNs can help.
concepts.example: Forward and backward RNNs on text.
concepts.misconception: That combining copies of the same model helps much; diversity is the point.

The reversed batch: newest timestep first.

math.numerical_example: For a sequence with 3 timesteps of temperatures [5, 7, 9] (oldest to newest), the reversed sequence is [9, 7, 5]; the target (the temperature 24 hours after the 9) is unchanged.

deeper.title: Running the reversed-order experiment in this edition
deeper.body:
Beyond the book. Since the datasets here are `tf.data` datasets from `timeseries_dataset_from_array` (p.382), not a generator, you reverse them with `map`:

```python
reverse = lambda x, y: (x[:, ::-1, :], y)
train_rev = train_dataset.map(reverse)
val_rev = val_dataset.map(reverse)
test_rev = test_dataset.map(reverse)

inputs = keras.Input(shape=(sequence_length, raw_data.shape[-1]))
x = layers.LSTM(16)(inputs)
outputs = layers.Dense(1)(x)
model = keras.Model(inputs, outputs)
model.compile(optimizer="adam", loss="mse", metrics=["mae"])
model.fit(train_rev, epochs=10, validation_data=val_rev)
```

Based on the page, expect a validation MAE worse than the baseline's 2.44 (the book gives no exact number). Alternatively, `layers.LSTM(16, go_backwards=True)` makes the layer itself read the sequence in reverse.

deeper.title: Why the reversed LSTM loses: a distance argument
deeper.body:
An inference from the page's explanation, made concrete:

1. The commonsense baseline shows the single most predictive input is the latest temperature, at timestep 120.
2. Chronological LSTM: timestep 120 is read last, 0 steps before the output; it enters the final state almost undiluted.
3. Reversed LSTM: timestep 120 is read first, 119 steps before the output; to use it, the LSTM must carry it through 119 updates, while inputs from five days ago (least predictive) are freshest in its state.
4. LSTMs can carry information far, but imperfectly; the result is a model that cannot even match 'copy the latest temperature'.

For text classification the key cues may be anywhere, so step 3's penalty applies roughly equally in both directions.

deeper.title: Analogy: two readers of the same story
deeper.body: Imagine two people reading the same mystery novel, one from the first page, one from the last page backward. Each forms a different mental model (the page's own image is of living life with time flowing backward). If you want to guess the next chapter, the forward reader, who just read the latest events, is far better placed: that's the weather task. If you want to know what the book is about, both can do it, and comparing their notes gives a fuller picture than either alone: that's text, and that's the bidirectional RNN.

misconceptions.claim: A bidirectional RNN always beats a unidirectional one.
misconceptions.correction: The page says it helps 'on certain tasks'. On the weather task, the reversed direction strongly underperforms even the baseline, and p.402 shows the bidirectional LSTM doing worse than the plain LSTM.

misconceptions.claim: If order matters for a task, only one reading direction can work.
misconceptions.correction: On text, word order matters but which order you use isn't crucial: reversed processing works just as well.

misconceptions.claim: Reversing the sequence also requires reversing the target.
misconceptions.correction: Only the inputs are reversed (samples[:, ::-1, :]); the targets are yielded unchanged.

misconceptions.claim: A model trained on reversed text learns the same thing as one trained on forward text.
misconceptions.correction: It learns different representations; that difference, when both are useful, is what makes combining them valuable.

takeaways: A bidirectional RNN runs two regular RNNs over the same sequence, chronologically and antichronologically, and merges their representations.
RNNs are order dependent; this is why they suit forecasting and why two directions give two different views.
On the Jena task, an LSTM fed reversed sequences strongly underperforms even the commonsense baseline.
Reason: the LSTM remembers the recent past best, and recent weather data is the most predictive.
On text, reversed processing works as well as forward: order matters, but which order you use isn't crucial.
Different yet useful representations are always worth exploiting; this underlies bidirectional RNNs and ensembling.

questions.question: What happens when the first-experiment LSTM is trained on time-reversed Jena sequences?
options: It slightly beats the chronological LSTM
It strongly underperforms even the commonsense baseline
It fails to train at all
questions.answer: It strongly underperforms even the commonsense baseline
questions.explanation: This is the page's stated outcome; it shows chronological processing is important for this task. It trains, but poorly; it neither matches nor beats the forward LSTM.

questions.question: Give the two reasons the page offers for why the chronological LSTM is 'bound to outperform' the reversed one on weather data.
questions.answer: (1) The LSTM layer is typically better at remembering the recent past than the distant past; (2) the more recent weather data points are more predictive than older ones, which is also what makes the commonsense baseline strong. Read in reverse, the most predictive data is the furthest from the output.
questions.explanation: Both facts are stated on the page; together they mean the reversed model must remember the most important data across the longest distance.

questions.question: What does samples[:, ::-1, :] do to a batch of shape (batch, timesteps, features)?
questions.answer: It reverses the order of the timesteps (axis 1) in every sequence, leaving the batch and feature axes, and the targets, unchanged.
questions.explanation: ::-1 is a reversed slice applied only to the middle (time) axis.

questions.question: According to the page, why is reversed-order processing fine for natural language?
options: Because word order doesn't matter in language
Because a word's importance in understanding a sentence isn't strongly dependent on its position, so which order you use isn't crucial
Because text sequences are always short
Because LSTMs remember the distant past better on text
questions.answer: Because a word's importance in understanding a sentence isn't strongly dependent on its position, so which order you use isn't crucial
questions.explanation: The page explicitly says word order does matter; what doesn't matter is the direction. Sequence length and memory claims are not the reasons given.

questions.question: If a reversed RNN on text performs about as well as a forward one, why would combining them help at all?
questions.answer: Because they learn different representations; different yet useful representations capture aspects missed by the other, so merging them can boost performance (the ensembling intuition, p.402).
questions.explanation: Equal accuracy does not mean identical features or identical errors.

questions.question: Based on this page alone, would you expect a bidirectional LSTM to beat the plain LSTM on the Jena task? Why or why not?
questions.answer: No: the antichronological half is severely underperforming on this task (worse than the baseline), so nearly all predictive power must come from the chronological half, while the extra half adds capacity. p.402 confirms it doesn't perform as well and overfits earlier.
questions.explanation: This prediction follows from the reversed-order experiment and is confirmed by Listing 13.24's results.

questions.question: Can you think of a sequence task of your own where reading order is crucial and one where it is not? Which would benefit from a bidirectional RNN?
questions.answer: Example: forecasting tomorrow's stock volume from the last 30 days (order and direction matter; bidirectional unlikely to help) vs. classifying the sentiment of a review (direction not crucial; bidirectional likely to help).
questions.explanation: The test is whether the useful information is concentrated at one end of the sequence (direction matters) or spread throughout (direction doesn't).
